title: Iowa's Lead Blast: What Happened, the Science and the Food Question
bluf: As of Friday night, EPA has not released any soil, dust or water results from the Iowa lead blast. It says the first numbers will post at epa.gov/IowaData starting tonight. Air monitors ran 30 hours after the blast and found no airborne lead before shutting off Thursday afternoon. Crews have taken about 1,600 samples before the blast and about as many after, and EPA says it sampled farms with USDA both times. Online, the mood has swung from alarm to relief, and the fight has moved to blame and to whether the ground results will match the air. Nothing yet shows lead reached food, but no food test data is public.
caution: Officials report good news so far, but it covers the air only. Every line carries a source and a status. Treat claims from any side, official or online, as claims until test numbers are public.

EPA ended air monitoring at 3pm CT Thursday after 30 hours with no airborne lead.
Baseline sample count corrected. The 1,200 in Update 1 was an early tally. EPA now cites 1,591 to 1,639 samples before the blast.
EPA says it sampled farms with USDA before and after, and is testing Missouri farm ponds. CDC sent a toxicology team.
One trade site reports the Army will clean yards above 200 ppm lead. Not confirmed elsewhere.
New: White House internal questions per CBS, Rob Sand's call for transparency, the lawsuit continuing, and the data center claim PolitiFact checked.
New sections: past cases (Notre Dame, East Palestine, Camp Minden, Radford, Herculaneum), more science, foreign and state media coverage.

confirmed.text: No post blast soil, dust or water results were public as of Friday evening. EPA said they would start posting Friday night.

EPA finished 88% of after blast sampling at homes it tested before.
EPA says it sampled nearby farms with USDA both before and after the blast, and is testing Missouri farm ponds.

reported.text: CDC activated an emergency response with a toxicology team to help Iowa's health department.
CBS sources say the chaotic lead up reached the White House and prompted internal questions about blame.
Winds pushed any dust toward northern Missouri, so Illinois effects look minimal.

timeline.event: EPA placed the plant on the National Priorities List (the Superfund list) because explosives had polluted surface water beyond the fence.
State sampling of 53 nearby homes found the explosive RDX (an explosive) above the health advisory level in some private wells. The Army supplies bottled water to affected homes.
Army officials say decay of the stored lead azide was first noticed in an annual check.
Army told EPA it found 68 drums of possibly unstable lead azide in plant bunkers during routine checks. The plant paused operations for a safety review.
timeline.source: ABC News timeline; Des Moines Register

timeline.event: Joint Munitions Command said the safety review concerned lead azide, a compound once used in blasting caps that the plant no longer needs.
Plant reopened after an 18 day closure. About 800 people work there.
timeline.source: Des Moines Register via AOL; ABC News

timeline.event: EPA issued the first emergency storage permit, reclassifying the drums as hazardous waste.
EPA posted public notice of the first emergency storage permit.
EPA Region 7 issued a second emergency storage permit, good through Sep 28. EPA said recrystallization made the material more sensitive to friction and shock. It took no public comments.
EPA settled a hazardous waste case (docket RCRA-07-2024-0092) with the Army and operator American Ordnance. They paid $39,311 for 2023 violations, including open burning above permit limits.
EPA issued a third emergency storage permit covering storage through Dec 26. It was published Nov 3 and did not authorize a blast.
Army said moving the drums off site was an unacceptable risk and it would detonate them on site in November.
About 200 residents attended an Army open house with plant commander Lt. Col. Daniel Nosse.
timeline.source: ABC News timeline; Task and Purpose

timeline.event: Army says it met with Middletown officials before the public announcement.
timeline.source: Task and Purpose, quoting Army spokesperson Justine Barati

timeline.event: EPA issued the emergency permit for an on site, controlled detonation. It expires Feb 11, 2027. It requires public notice, sampling before and after, cleanup and reports.
Army advisory set two blasts for Nov 20 around noon CT and asked residents near Middletown City Park to leave because windows could break.
timeline.source: ABC News timeline; Iowa Public Radio

timeline.event: EPA published the permit notice and sent a field team to sample. The governor's office says this Monday was when the state first learned of the plan.
timeline.source: Earthjustice motion; Iowa Public Radio; States Newsroom

timeline.event: Illinois EPA said EPA Region 7 never notified it. Illinois urged air, soil and dust sampling in western Illinois. The Army posted its environmental assessment the same day.
timeline.source: Illinois Department of Public Health release

timeline.event: Earthjustice filed a petition and emergency motion in the 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals for the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club Iowa Chapter to block the permit.
Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle moved the blast to Nov 23. He said he wanted the latest point before a forecast cold snap, since cold makes the material less stable.
The 8th Circuit granted a temporary administrative stay of the permit while it weighed the motion.
Army, EPA and federal HHS issued a joint statement describing extra mitigation measures.
Justice Department told the court the Army would proceed even without the permit, citing an emergency exemption and higher blast risk in freezing weather. ABC reports differ on the date.
timeline.source: ABC News timeline and Nov 22 report

timeline.event: Army moved the blast to Nov 25 for better weather and to finish mitigation. Nearby residents taped windows.
President Trump said he ordered the military to hold off until the appeals court and governor elect Rob Sand approved.
8th Circuit denied the emergency motion and lifted the stay. It said an uncontrolled explosion posed the greater danger.
Telle set the blast for about 9am CT Nov 25. Army recommended evacuating Middletown and a 5 mile cone southwest of the plant. Up to 100 Iowa National Guard troops assisted.
timeline.source: ABC News timeline; Yahoo News live

timeline.event: Gov. Kim Reynolds declared a disaster emergency for Des Moines, Lee and Van Buren counties. Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe opened his state emergency center.
timeline.source: ABC News timeline; Yahoo News live

timeline.event: Iowa HHS said it does not recommend widespread blood lead tests yet. Targeted testing will depend on soil and dust results.
FEMA alert told everyone within 20 miles to shelter in place and said evacuation was no longer advised.
FAA closed the airspace around the plant through 12:52pm CT.
Army set off two rapid blasts. Video showed two white plumes. Army said the smoke was foam sprayed on the bunkers.
Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe said mitigation appeared successful and the blast was well contained.
Reporters saw two NASA research aircraft overhead collecting air pollution data.
Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley said all 68 drums were destroyed with no secondary explosions. AP reports this was the nation's entire lead azide stockpile.

timeline.time: Nov 25, just after 6:30pm (time zone not stated)
timeline.event: All clear issued. Joint FEMA and Army statement said air monitoring showed no detectable lead. Army said defense agency maps showed zero airborne lead.
Army said surface sampling is underway with results released once complete. A Purdue engineer said lab results take days to weeks.

The Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club Iowa Chapter and Earthjustice said they will keep pressing the Army and EPA to monitor and clean up. They want an account of how the lead azide decayed and why the public learned so late.
timeline.source: KGAN CBS 2 Iowa; Iowa Environmental Council statement

timeline.event: The Iowa Environmental Council says its lawsuit against the EPA permit is still moving through the 8th Circuit. ABC reports the groups said they would not try further to block the blast itself.
timeline.source: Iowa Environmental Council statement; ABC News

timeline.event: Earthjustice said it will keep weighing strategies to ensure proper cleanup. It named no specific next legal step.
ATF Director Robert Cekada said the blast was directed into the ground along a designed channel to limit spread into the air.
USDA set up a response email inbox and resource page. Local Farm Service Agency and conservation offices are helping farmers. Secretary Brooke Rollins said the food supply is safe.
timeline.source: Food World News, citing a USDA release

timeline.event: EPA regional administrator Jim Macy told Iowa's governor that first dust wipe results would come in the days after the blast. A full data review will take longer.

University of Iowa's Patrick O'Shaughnessy was pulling air through filters for lab lead tests, with help from Oregon and New York researchers. His group hoped to share early data Nov 26. No release was found.
Cleanup at the blast site is expected to take about three months. Up to 13 tons of debris may need hazardous waste disposal.
An early EPA tally listed 1,216 baseline samples: 650 soil, 297 dust, 210 water and 59 air.

EPA said its real time monitors still showed zero airborne lead. It said it took 1,591 air, water, soil and dust samples before the blast and more than 1,000 since. Teams sampled schools, playgrounds, day care centers and churches.
EPA said it also plans to test for volatile organic compounds and fine particles, not only lead. It said it will stay on the ground as long as needed.
timeline.source: ABC News; AP via MPR News

timeline.event: Governor elect Rob Sand said the lead up was chaotic and unclear and called for immediate transparency. He said affected Iowans must be taken care of. He deferred to the Trump administration on the federal operation.
Shaw Local reported that northeast winds pushed any dust cloud into northern Missouri. It said any direct effect on Illinois looks minimal.
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker told state agencies, including Illinois EPA, to stay on alert until the Army finishes and EPA sampling is complete.
EPA said soil, water and dust results from a lab in Kansas City, Kansas, could come as early as Friday. About 300 EPA staff are sampling across the region.

Citing The New York Times, Shaw Local reported the Army approached MuniRem Environmental in March about chemical dissolving and canceled in May. The reported reason was that moving the barrels raised the risk of ignition.
timeline.source: Shaw Local citing The New York Times

timeline.event: EPA ended air monitoring after 30 hours of readings. No airborne lead was detected.
timeline.source: KGAN CBS 2 Iowa, citing an EPA Facebook update

timeline.event: EPA said it took 1,591 air, water, soil and dust samples before the blast. Earlier official counts were about 1,200, and CBS says more than 1,600.
EPA said it had taken more than 1,000 samples after the blast, starting about 1pm CT on Nov 25. More than 130 structures sampled before were sampled again.
EPA said it sampled nearby farms together with USDA both before and after the blast. It is also sampling farm ponds in Missouri.
Samples went to EPA's regional lab in Kansas City, Kansas, three mobile labs on site, one air toxics lab and private contract labs. About 300 EPA staff and contractors were deployed.
EPA put out canisters to catch volatile chemicals at 4am CT on blast day and collected them 24 hours later. It is also testing for fine particles.
EPA said its real time air monitors still showed zero airborne lead. It expected the first lab results on samples taken after the blast as early as Nov 27.
timeline.source: EPA news release; AP via MPR News

timeline.event: Schools, playgrounds, daycares and churches were on EPA's sampling list for Nov 26, plus a second round of drinking water tests.
ABC News reports the CDC activated an emergency response to support Iowa's health department, including a toxicology team.
ABC News reports the Army's guidance put the possible hazardous dust zone at 148 square miles outside the plant.
Iowa's agriculture department had advised moving cattle, feed and equipment elsewhere or indoors, while saying that may not be possible on every farm.
FEMA short term hotel lodging for evacuees runs through Friday Nov 27.
EPA said it had finished 88% of after blast sampling at homes it also sampled before. It expected to finish the rest that day.

EPA totals rose to 1,639 samples before the blast and 1,618 after. Crews assessed 187 sites, including homes, schools, playgrounds, churches and day care centers. Crews enter private land only with permission.
EPA said results will be posted at epa.gov/IowaData as they come in. Exact sample locations may be added to its online map later, after staff verify them.
EPA expected to begin releasing soil, dust and water results Friday night. No after blast lab numbers were found in any source opened as of this time.
CBS News sources said the chaotic lead up reached the White House. It prompted internal questions about what went wrong and who was to blame.
University of Iowa engineering professor David Cwiertny cautioned that real time air readings cannot replace lab analysis. Independent researchers are also testing soil and dust.
Lindsay James, described as a newly elected congresswoman, demanded accountability and assurances it will not recur. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said EPA will clean up if needed.
EPA said it had finished 88 percent of the after blast sampling at homes it also sampled before, and expected to finish the rest that day.
No lab results from after the blast had been made public. No crop, hay, milk, egg or meat results had been released either.
A trade site reports the Army will clean up home yards that test above 200 milligrams of lead per kilogram of soil, at government cost. No second source was found.
EPA detonation permit expires. Its Condition Q.2 requires a final report on dust dispersion and ground deposition.

hypotheses.name: Was the public told enough and in time?
hypotheses.summary: The Army announced the plan in October. State officials say they learned the details only days before.

for.point: New: After the blast EPA gave daily public updates with sample counts and promised results at epa.gov/IowaData as they arrive.
Army announced on Oct 8 it would blast on site in November and held an Oct 15 open house for about 200 residents.
EPA posted public notices of the storage permits in May and July.
Army said the permit required notice within 105 miles and that it met Middletown officials Nov 12.
The blast was delayed twice, giving six more days of notice, and the Army updated plume maps hourly before the event.
for.source: ABC News; Iowa HHS fact sheet

against.point: New: EPA's baseline sample count shifted across updates, from 1,200 to 1,591 to 1,639, without explanation in coverage.
New: CBS sources say the confusion reached the White House and set off internal questions about blame.
New: The groups say the Army knew of decay since 2009 and instability since March, yet most Iowans learned days before Nov 20.
New: Governor elect Rob Sand said the lead up was chaotic and unclear.
The governor's office says Iowa learned of the blast plan Nov 16, four days before the first date.
Illinois EPA said EPA Region 7 never notified it, though Army maps showed dust reaching western Illinois.
Iowa HHS said it was only very recently made aware of the plan.
EPA took no public comments on the storage permits and, per the lawsuit, skipped the 45 day comment period for the blast permit.
Governor elect Rob Sand called it an unacceptable lack of communication and clarity.
University of Iowa researchers had not been told how monitoring would work, a day before the first date.

unknowns: Why EPA Region 7 did not alert Iowa and Illinois sooner

hypotheses.name: Was detonation the safest option?
hypotheses.summary: The Army, EPA and an appeals court said a planned blast beat a random one. Critics say other options were not tested.

for.point: New: Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley said all barrels were destroyed with no secondary blasts or damage to buildings.
New: The Army said the stockpile was degrading and might explode on its own as weather got colder.
EPA found the degraded material an imminent and substantial threat of spontaneous explosion.
Army's environmental assessment rejected chemical neutralization and transport as too dangerous. Crystals on drum lids made opening or moving them unsafe.
The 8th Circuit found an uncontrolled explosion more harmful than the planned one.
All 68 drums were destroyed with no secondary explosions, and witnesses said the blasts were smaller than expected.

against.point: New: The environmental groups say the Army has not explained why the material decayed. They credit their lawsuit with forcing extra safeguards.
New: The Army reportedly dropped a chemical dissolving option from MuniRem in May. Shaw Local says it is unclear what other options were weighed.
against.source: Shaw Local citing The New York Times

against.point: The groups say the Army never evaluated mobile treatment units and dismissed a neutralization product EPA lists for lead azide without data.
A University of Iowa professor emeritus called the situation a case of neglect that left only bad options.
ATF (federal explosives bureau) director Robert Cekada said the stockpile was moved to Iowa from bases nationwide in 2009, so it sat for years before action.

unknowns: Whether a chemical treatment was ever tested on a sample

hypotheses.name: Did lead leave the plant in harmful amounts?
hypotheses.summary: Air monitors found nothing in 30 hours. About 1,600 ground samples are in labs. First results due Friday night.

for.point: New: EPA resampled 88% of homes it tested before the blast by Friday, giving a direct before and after comparison.
New: ATF's director said the blast was channeled into the ground to limit spread into the air.
New: EPA ran air monitors for 30 hours after the blast and detected no airborne lead before shutting them off Thursday afternoon.
Joint FEMA and Army statement said all air monitoring showed no detectable lead. Army said defense agency maps showed zero airborne lead.
Mitigation included water walls of eight 16,000 gallon tanks, gel blocks, sand barriers and PFAS free (no "forever chemicals") foam to trap dust.
Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe said the blast was well contained.
EPA says all real time air monitors showed zero detectable airborne lead more than five hours after the blast, and the Army reported a 0.0 ground reading.
Containment included concrete and earth covered magazines, two story sand barriers, eight 16,000 gallon water tanks, gel blocks, misters and foam. Officials said the blast caved inward.
EPA says it holds 1,200 baseline samples taken before the blast, which lets it compare before and after.

against.point: New: A University of Iowa engineer said real time readings cannot replace detailed lab analysis.
New: Shaw Local said it is still unclear whether the plume carried lead toward homes and farms. Winds pushed any dust toward northern Missouri.
New: No soil, dust or water lab results were public as of Friday evening. Settled dust is not measured by air monitors.
Purdue's Andrew Whelton said air data look promising but lab tests of samples are needed and take days to weeks.
Iowa HHS said the airborne all clear does not end precautions about settled dust. No safe lead level is known.
Before the blast, a University of Iowa professor said the Army never showed expected settled dust levels. Another said hosing moves lead into soil and water.
The permit's soil cleanup bar of 800 parts per million is four times EPA's current 200 level, the groups say.
A Donnellson livestock farmer questioned the accuracy of EPA's monitors.

The Army map gave no projected surface dust amounts, and independent researchers said they had no details on monitor locations or instruments.
In the plant's 1970s open air detonation, about a quarter of the lead azide went airborne.

hypotheses.name: Is food from the area safe?
hypotheses.summary: Officials say yes. EPA and USDA sampled farms before and after. No food data is public yet.

for.point: New: EPA and USDA sampled farms both before and after the blast, so direct comparisons are possible.
New: EPA's real time air monitors showed zero airborne lead since the blast, at four sites.
New: USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins said the food supply is safe and that USDA and FDA have rules to keep heavy metals out of it.
Iowa Agriculture Secretary Mike Naig said officials do not expect harm to livestock health from the blast, based on current data.
Farmers had days of warning to house animals, cover feed and water, and take baseline samples, following Iowa State guidance.

New: Iowa State's beef specialist warned lead poisoning in cattle can show up later as fertility problems.
New: No forage, feed, livestock, milk or egg results have been published. Officials have not released the tests behind their assurances.
USDA projected about 350 farms under the plume, and no crop, hay, milk or egg test results have been released.
Iowa State warned stored feed, pasture and pond water may stay a risk longer than the airborne period. Lead also passes from cows to calves through milk.

unknowns: Crop, hay, milk, egg and meat test results

hypotheses.name: What are the long term risks?
hypotheses.summary: Depends on what settled in soil and water. Results will decide.

for.point: New: After Notre Dame burned in 2019, French health officials tested 1,222 children and found no fire related rise in blood lead.
New: Peter Thorne of the University of Iowa said cancer is not the main concern for low level environmental lead.
New: An expert told Iowa Public Radio groundwater contamination is almost not a concern because soil holds lead near the surface.
The Army says it does not anticipate long term health effects and must clean up any soil above regulatory limits. It offers voluntary sampling of private property.
A University of Iowa researcher said the airborne plume would likely clear within hours, ending the main breathing risk quickly.

against.point: New: Drone tests at Radford Army Ammunition Plant found lead about five times the expected level in one burn type. Models can undercount metals.
New: A study of Notre Dame fallout found most excess lead landed within 1 km downwind. Limited blood testing left peak exposure poorly documented.
New: CDC says no safe blood lead level in children has been found. Its 3.5 reference value only flags the highest 2.5 percent.
New: Lead is an element and does not break down. Rinsing surfaces moves it into soil where small children play.
Health agencies say no safe level of lead has been identified for children. Long term low doses can harm brain development, and adults can get kidney damage and high blood pressure.

Rinsing surfaces moves lead into soil and surface water rather than removing it, a University of Iowa expert said. The Army's own assessment says lead could reach waterways through runoff or groundwater.

unknowns: Whether any soil tops the 800 ppm permit bar or EPA's 200 ppm level

extraSections.title: The Science
extraSections.intro: What lead azide is, what a blast does to it, and how lead affects people.

items.headline: What lead azide is
items.summary: Lead azide is a lead and nitrogen compound. It is a primary explosive, the very sensitive kind used to set off bigger charges in detonators and blasting caps. Its use started declining in the 1980s.

items.headline: Why these drums got more dangerous
items.summary: The drums sat about 20 years in earth covered bunkers, under a bath of ethanol and water to keep the powder stable. Some of that liquid evaporated and the lead azide formed crystals. Crystals make it more sensitive to shock and friction.
items.assessment: Army officials say decay was first noticed in a 2009 check. That gap is why critics call this neglect, not bad luck.

items.headline: Why the Army would not move or dissolve it
items.summary: The Army's environmental assessment ruled out trucking the drums away or neutralizing them with chemicals. Crystals on the drum lids made opening or moving them unsafe. The acting Army secretary also said cold weather makes the material less stable, so he wanted it done before a cold snap.
items.assessment: Opponents say a chemical treatment and mobile treatment units were never seriously tested. The appeals court sided with the Army on Nov 23.

items.headline: How much lead was in it
items.summary: Lead makes up about 71% of lead azide by weight. So about 10,000 pounds of it holds roughly 7,100 pounds of lead. This is Brief's arithmetic from the chemical formula, not an official figure. The drums also held liquid, so the real amount may be lower.
items.source: Brief arithmetic; tonnage from Fox News live coverage

items.headline: What a blast does to it
items.summary: When lead azide explodes it breaks apart into nitrogen gas and lead. The lead can then react with air and form fine particles that travel as dust. This is general chemistry. Officials have not released particle size or deposition numbers.
items.source: General chemistry; gap noted by The Intercept

items.headline: How they tried to trap the dust
items.summary: The Army surrounded the bunkers with water walls from eight 16,000 gallon tanks, gel blocks, tall sand barriers, misters and soaked soil. Fire trucks sprayed more than 3,600 gallons of foam. Officials say the white clouds on video were mostly that foam.

items.headline: How lead harms the body
items.summary: Health agencies say no safe level of lead has been found for children. Small doses over time can harm brain development. Adults can get kidney and blood pressure problems. The main risks here are breathing dust and swallowing settled dust.

items.headline: Why zero in the air is not the full answer
items.summary: The airborne all clear covers what is floating now. It does not show what settled on soil, roofs, ponds and fields in the first hour. Purdue engineer Andrew Whelton says the air data look promising but lab tests take days to weeks.
items.assessment: The question has moved from the air to the ground. Watch for soil and dust numbers against the cleanup bar.

items.headline: Before and after comparisons are possible
items.summary: EPA says it took 1,200 land, air, dust and water samples before the blast. That gives a baseline to compare against. None of the after results are public yet.

items.headline: Lead does not go away once it lands
items.summary: Lead is an element, so it does not decompose. Hosing off playground equipment moves it into soil. A University of Iowa expert said groundwater is a small worry because soil holds lead near the surface.
items.assessment: New in Update 2.

items.headline: What the Army predicted on the ground
items.summary: The Army's map showed a light coating of 5 micrograms of lead per square foot and a heavier 100 near the site. EPA's indoor cleanup standards are 5 for floors and 10 for windowsills. Dust was expected to pass in under an hour.
items.assessment: New in Update 2.

items.headline: How the samples get tested
items.summary: Real time monitors read airborne lead on the spot. Filters, dust wipes and soil go to EPA's Kansas City lab, three mobile labs and private labs. Canisters catch volatile chemicals over 24 hours. Purdue's Andrew Whelton says full results take days to weeks.
items.assessment: New in Update 2.

items.headline: What CDC's blood lead number means
items.summary: CDC's reference value is 3.5 micrograms per deciliter, set in October 2021. It marks the top 2.5 percent of US children aged 1 to 5. It is a screening flag, not a safe level.
items.assessment: New in Update 2.

items.headline: How far lead fallout traveled after Notre Dame
items.summary: Researchers estimate about 150 kg of lead went airborne in the 2019 fire. Airborne lead rose about twentyfold 50 km downwind. But most excess lead in soil landed within 1 km.
items.assessment: New in Update 2.

items.headline: Why models can undercount metals
items.summary: In 2016 an EPA designed drone sampled open burns at Radford Army Ammunition Plant in Virginia. Lead came out about five times the expected rate in one burn type, and arsenic far higher.
items.assessment: New in Update 2.

items.headline: A trench meant to steer the blast
items.summary: ATF's Robert Cekada said a blast channel was designed to limit lead spread. Earlier reporting described water walls, gel blocks, sand barriers and 3,600 gallons of foam to knock dust down.
items.assessment: New in Update 2.

extraSections.title: Food and Farms
extraSections.intro: What it means for livestock, crops and the food from this part of Iowa.

items.headline: EPA and USDA sampled farms before and after the blast
items.summary: EPA said it sampled nearby farms with USDA both before and after the blast. It is also testing farm ponds in Missouri, where the plume was forecast to head.
items.assessment: This is the first official sign that farm level baseline data exist. Nothing says when farmers will see their own results.

items.headline: Farmers still wait for soil, water and forage results
items.summary: Food World News, a food trade site, says no forage, feed or livestock test results have been published. It lists Iowa State's warning signs of lead poisoning in cattle, from blindness to later fertility problems.
items.assessment: No packer, dairy, egg buyer, elevator or vet lab statement turned up in any source. Silence from buyers is a useful signal in itself.

items.headline: A Donnellson cattle farmer fears for his pregnant herd
items.summary: Doug Seyb, a livestock farmer, told Australia's public broadcaster he doubts EPA's air monitors. He said all his cows are pregnant and he hopes for no stillborn calves. Iowa's agriculture department had advised moving cattle and feed indoors where possible.
items.assessment: Lead can cross to calves, so the worry is not only about meat. Calving season results would be a delayed indicator.

items.headline: CDC sent a toxicology team to help Iowa
items.summary: ABC News reports the CDC activated an emergency response to support Iowa's health department, including toxicologists. Iowa had asked for field help before the blast.
items.assessment: Federal help on the health side sits alongside Iowa's choice to hold off on mass blood lead tests. Watch whether CDC input changes that.

items.headline: Army reportedly will clean yards above 200 parts per million lead
items.summary: A trade site says the Army will clean up home yards testing above 200 milligrams of lead per kilogram, at government cost. That matches EPA's stricter screening level, not the 800 figure critics flagged in the permit.
items.assessment: If confirmed, it answers a main lawsuit complaint. Only one source carried it, so treat it as unconfirmed.

items.headline: University of Iowa team tested topsoil before and after
items.summary: David Cwiertny, who runs a state funded University of Iowa contamination center, said his team set air filters and took topsoil before the blast. They planned to resample the same spots afterward and test wipes in their own lab.
items.assessment: This is the main independent dataset that could check EPA's numbers. No release date was given.

items.headline: Deer shotgun season opens Dec 5 with no blast advice found
items.summary: Iowa's first shotgun deer season runs Dec 5 to 9 and the second Dec 12 to 20. No state advice on venison from the plume area was found.
items.assessment: Deer graze the same pasture farmers were told to avoid. Hunters will ask before any official test of wild game exists.

items.headline: Blast site cleanup will take about three months
items.summary: Permit details reported by NBC say site cleanup should take about three months. Up to 13 tons of debris may need hazardous waste disposal. The crater was expected to be about 38 feet wide.
items.assessment: The site itself stays a lead source during cleanup. Rain and wind over that period matter for nearby farms.

items.headline: Iowa Farmers Union says USDA came late to the blast
items.summary: Aaron Lehman, president of the Iowa Farmers Union, said USDA responded late and cited cuts to local food programs and county staff. Secretary Brooke Rollins posted that she hears worried producers. A USDA spokesperson said there is no risk to the food supply.
items.assessment: The farm story is shifting from contamination fear to a fight over USDA capacity. That frame will outlast the test results.

items.headline: USDA says the food supply is safe
items.summary: USDA officials said the food supply is safe while more soil, water and livestock testing goes on. No food test results were published with that statement.
items.assessment: This is an official assurance, not yet a data release. It would firm up once crop, milk and meat results are public.

items.headline: Iowa's farm chief expects no harm to livestock
items.summary: Mike Naig, Iowa's Secretary of Agriculture, said officials do not expect harm to livestock health, based on current information.

items.headline: About 350 farms sat under the expected plume
items.summary: USDA projected about 350 farms could be under the plume, per Iowa's health agency. Des Moines County alone had more than 51,000 cattle, hogs, sheep, goats, horses and hens in 2022. Within 20 miles the count may top 70,000.

items.headline: What farmers were told to do
items.summary: Iowa State University's Beef Center told producers to pull cattle off pasture and pond water for a few days. It said to cover tanks and feed, drain and rinse open tanks, and blow dust off hay bales. It suggested baseline soil, forage and blood samples before and after.
items.assessment: Standing pond water was flagged as the bigger risk. Animals drink it for days after dust settles.

items.headline: Most crops were already in
items.summary: Iowa State's Dirk Maier, a grain storage expert, said most crops in the area were already harvested and stored before the blast. That limits how much grain was exposed in the field. Pasture, hay, ponds and gardens are the bigger concern.

items.headline: Lead can pass from cows to calves
items.summary: Iowa State warned stored feed, pasture and pond water may stay a risk longer than the airborne period. Lead also passes from cows to calves through milk.

items.headline: Egg farmer in Maquoketa area pays for her own soil and water tests
items.summary: Margaret Zimmerman, who keeps egg laying chickens on about 36 acres northeast of the plant, told KCRG she felt poorly informed. She is paying for soil and water tests before and after the blast. An Army map showed her land in the possible exposure zone.
items.assessment: Private baseline tests by farmers could become an independent check on the official data.

items.headline: No crop, hay, milk or egg results yet
items.summary: No test results for crops, hay, milk, eggs or meat had been released as of Wednesday night. Iowa HHS is holding off on mass blood lead testing until soil and dust results come in.

extraSections.title: Key Numbers
extraSections.intro: Figures from officials and reporting. Arithmetic is labeled.

items.headline: Samples before the blast: 1,591
items.summary: EPA count. Earlier White House figure was 1,200. CBS says more than 1,600.

items.headline: Samples after the blast (by Nov 26): More than 1,000
items.summary: EPA count, from about 1pm CT Nov 25

items.headline: Structures resampled: More than 130
items.summary: EPA figure

items.headline: Structures sampled (CBS figure): More than 180
items.summary: CBS article text. Its own page summary says 130. Likely different counting.

items.headline: Home resampling done by Nov 27: 88 percent
items.summary: EPA via CBS

items.headline: EPA staff and contractors: About 300
items.summary: Plus 170 pieces of equipment and 3 mobile labs

items.headline: Possible hazardous dust zone: 148 square miles
items.summary: Army guidance via ABC News

items.headline: Reported yard cleanup trigger: 200 mg/kg lead
items.summary: Single trade site source. Not confirmed.

items.headline: CDC blood lead reference value: 3.5 µg/dL
items.summary: Top 2.5 percent of US kids aged 1 to 5. Not a safe level.

items.headline: Blast site debris: Up to 13 tons
items.summary: May need hazardous waste disposal. Cleanup about three months.

items.headline: Lead inside the lead azide: About 7,100 lb (3.5 short tons)
items.summary: Labeled arithmetic, not from a source. Lead azide, Pb(N3)2, has a molar mass of about 291, and lead (207) is about 71 percent of it. 0.71 x 10,000 lb is about 7,100 lb. Using the 9,700 lb net explosive weight gives about 6,900 lb. The drums also held ethanol and water, so the real figure may be lower.

items.headline: Share airborne in the 1970s open air detonation: About 25 percent
items.summary: Single local TV report. Applied to today's lead content that would be roughly 1,700 lb with no containment (labeled arithmetic). This blast had sand, water, gel and foam barriers.

items.headline: Farms projected under the plume: About 350
items.summary: USDA projection cited by Iowa HHS. Not confirmed contamination.

items.headline: Livestock in Des Moines County: More than 51,000 (2022)
items.summary: Cattle, hogs, sheep, goats, horses and hens, per USDA data. Possibly over 70,000 within 20 miles.

items.headline: EPA nears end of home resampling, first lab results due
items.summary: EPA said Friday it had finished 88% of after blast sampling at homes it tested before the Nov 25 blast. It said lab results would start coming out Friday night at epa.gov/IowaData. As of Friday evening no soil, dust or water numbers had been published.
items.assessment: Matched before and after samples at the same homes give the strongest test of whether dust landed. Watch whether EPA posts raw values by location or only a summary.

items.headline: EPA ends air monitoring after 30 hours with no lead found
items.summary: EPA shut down its air monitors at 3pm CT Thursday after 30 hours of readings. It said no airborne lead was detected. The agency also said it is testing for other chemicals the blast could release.
items.assessment: This closes the air question for now. It leaves the ground question open, since settled dust is what officials say drives health risk.
items.source: KGAN CBS 2 Iowa; AP via MPR News

items.headline: EPA sample counts change from update to update
items.summary: Before the blast EPA cited 1,200 baseline samples. Later updates said 1,591, then more than 1,600, then 1,639. After blast counts went from more than 1,000 to 1,618, and sites from more than 130 to 187.
items.assessment: Rising totals likely reflect more sampling, not errors. Still, the exact baseline matters when comparing before and after values, so the final count should be pinned down.
items.source: KGAN CBS 2 Iowa; ABC News; CBS News

items.headline: White House asked what went wrong, CBS sources say
items.summary: CBS News reported, citing unnamed sources, that the chaotic lead up reached the White House. It said it prompted internal questions about what went wrong and who was to blame. President Trump has publicly praised the result.
items.assessment: Public praise and private blame hunting can run together. If an internal review exists, it could shape who answers to Congress in January.

items.headline: Rob Sand calls the run up chaotic and asks for transparency
items.summary: Governor elect Rob Sand, a Democrat who takes office in January, said the lead up to the blast should not have been so confusing. He called for immediate transparency and care for affected Iowans. He deferred to the Trump administration on the federal operation itself.
items.assessment: Sand is framing this as a process failure, not a health disaster. That leaves him room to push for answers without contradicting the reassuring air data.

items.headline: Environmental groups say their permit lawsuit goes on
items.summary: The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club Iowa Chapter, represented by Earthjustice, say their challenge to the EPA permit is still in the 8th Circuit. Director Sarah Green told Shaw Local the council will continue legal action. They want a full accounting of why it reached a crisis.
items.assessment: With the blast done, the live legal issue is cleanup. The permit's terms, including its cleanup level, are what the case can still affect.
items.source: Iowa Environmental Council statement; Shaw Local

items.headline: Wind carried any dust toward Missouri, not Illinois
items.summary: Shaw Local, a northern Illinois news group, reported northeast winds pushed any dust into northern Missouri. It said any direct effect on Illinois looks minimal. Gov. JB Pritzker kept Illinois agencies on alert until EPA sampling ends.
items.assessment: If dust drifted, northeast Missouri is where to look. No Missouri soil results were found, so that state's testing is the missing piece.

items.headline: ATF chief says the blast was steered into the ground
items.summary: Robert Cekada, who runs the federal explosives bureau (ATF), said the blast went into the ground along a channel built to limit spread into the air. Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley said all barrels were destroyed with no damage to buildings.
items.assessment: Pushing the blast down helps explain zero airborne lead. It may also mean more lead stayed in soil on the plant, which matters for on site cleanup.

items.headline: Army reportedly dropped a chemical option in May
items.summary: Shaw Local, citing The New York Times, said the Army asked MuniRem Environmental in March about dissolving the lead azide chemically. The Army canceled in May, reportedly because moving the barrels raised the risk of ignition. It is unclear what other options were weighed.
items.assessment: This puts a date on when the Army chose detonation. Six months then passed before states were told, which is the gap oversight will likely probe.
items.source: Shaw Local citing The New York Times

items.headline: Iowa researcher warns air readings are not the final word
items.summary: David Cwiertny, a University of Iowa engineering professor, said real time readings cannot replace lab analysis. Lindsay James, described as a newly elected member of Congress, demanded accountability. EPA chief Lee Zeldin said EPA will clean up if needed.
items.assessment: Independent testers plan their own soil and dust work. Any gap between their numbers and EPA's would become the next big story.

items.headline: EPA says first lab results could arrive Friday
items.summary: EPA said Thursday it had taken 1,591 samples before the blast and more than 1,000 after. Samples went to its Kansas City lab, three mobile labs and private labs. It expected the first lab results as early as Friday.
items.assessment: The baseline count keeps changing between 1,200, 1,591 and more than 1,600. Ask which number the before and after comparisons will actually use.

items.headline: Scientists say air readings are not the final word
items.summary: Joel Kaufman, a University of Washington air pollution doctor, called zero airborne lead a promising sign. He said lab tests of settled dust in many places must back it up. Purdue engineer Andrew Whelton said settled particles must be collected and lab tested.
items.assessment: Experts on both sides agree on the test that matters. The dispute is only about whether to trust the result before it exists.

items.headline: Natural News says the success claim is premature
items.summary: Natural News, a health freedom site, ran a Nov 27 piece by Ramon Tomey. It says air results are clean but lead never breaks down and full effects take weeks. It cites AP, CBC and Iowa Capital Dispatch, plus the site's own AI tool for health claims.
items.assessment: The piece stops short of alleging a cover up. That restraint suggests the alt right is waiting for soil data before escalating.
items.support: It correctly notes soil and water results were still pending and that health agencies say no lead level is known to be safe.
items.against: Health claims lean on the site's own AI engine and affiliated videos, not independent experts. EPA has found no airborne lead.

items.headline: Epoch Times finds relieved, underwhelmed residents
items.summary: The Epoch Times, a right leaning paper, interviewed residents in Keokuk, Burlington and Fort Madison. Most said the blast was far smaller than feared. Two suggested the warnings were overstated.
items.assessment: This is the clearest record of the mood flip after the all clear. It also gives a voice to the idea that agencies overreact.
items.support: Residents' first hand views of a visibly small blast, plus FEMA's preliminary 0.0 air reading.
items.against: The paper reports the overstated warning view without testing it. Ground results were not yet in.

items.headline: Epoch Times reports 1,591 baseline samples and wider testing
items.summary: An Epoch Times piece on Nov 27 said EPA took 1,591 samples before the blast and more than 1,000 after. Sites include homes, parks, farms and drinking water intakes. Schools, daycares and churches come next, and EPA is also testing other compounds.
items.assessment: The baseline number is higher than the 1,200 the first edition carried. It gives a clearer yardstick for any later soil finding.
items.support: Specific sample counts and lab locations from EPA, and a quote from Earthjustice attorney Thien Chau.
items.against: No resident or independent scientist views. Relies fully on agency statements.

items.headline: Chinese language Epoch Times stresses Trump's praise and joking onlookers
items.summary: The Epoch Times Chinese edition led with Trump calling the blast PERFECT and onlookers chatting. It gave Trump's Obama era blame and his jab at Rob Sand, plus Sand's criticism.
items.assessment: This shows the pro administration framing reaching Chinese diaspora readers, a contrast to alarmed coverage inside China.
items.source: The Epoch Times Chinese edition (Ji Wei)
items.support: Draws on AP's on site reporting and named officials.
items.against: Leans toward the administration's account. Gives little space to pending ground tests.

items.headline: Mother Jones frames the blast as a military pattern of late warnings
items.summary: Mother Jones, a progressive magazine, said the Army forgot to warn people and listed past military contamination cases. It cited Camp Lejeune, Hanford and Radford, Virginia. It said Defense officials raised stockpile concerns as early as 2004.
items.assessment: Published Nov 19 and not carried before. It shows the left frame that now feeds the neglect narrative after the blast.
items.support: The 2004 concern is backed by a 2014 Army article, per PolitiFact. Iowa's governor did learn of the plan late.
items.against: Written before the blast and the zero air readings. PolitiFact says the 2004 concern may not match this year's hazard.

items.headline: Substack writer says blame came before information
items.summary: An independent Substack writer said Washington put more effort into blaming Obama and Rob Sand than informing families. He claimed an EPA hotline number aired on CNN had a wrong digit. Citing CBS, he said senior defense leaders were not briefed in March.
items.assessment: The hotline detail is small but checkable. If true, it would fit a wider story of rushed public communication.
items.support: Builds on named outlets, including CBS, and on officials' own conflicting statements.
items.against: The hotline claim was not verified by any outlet found. Most of the post is behind a paywall.

items.headline: Epidemiologist says officials fed fear by withholding context
items.summary: Katelyn Jetelina, an epidemiologist who writes Your Local Epidemiologist, said surface dust is the main risk and grain is minimal. She said science communicators online calmed fears that officials stoked by sharing numbers without context.
items.assessment: A researcher arguing that poor official communication, not creators, drove the panic. That flips the usual misinformation blame.
items.support: She cites a Science explainer and compares EPA soil levels with stricter California and scientist proposed limits.
items.against: Written before the blast results. She says the national food supply is not at risk, which some local voices dispute.

items.headline: PolitiFact finds no link between the blast and data centers
items.summary: PolitiFact checked X posts saying the Army wanted the land for data centers. It found no Army document on future land use. The nearby bitcoin site says it expands on land it already owns.
items.assessment: The real data center fight next door made the claim feel plausible. Expect it to return if land near the plant is sold.

items.headline: PolitiFact calls the 2004 warning claim unclear
items.summary: PolitiFact confirmed a 2014 Army article saying the Pentagon worried about the stockpile in 2004. It said officials give conflicting ages for the material. It is not clear the 2004 worry was the same hazard found in March.
items.assessment: This is the strongest documented fact behind the neglect narrative. It is also the one officials have not explained.

items.headline: Snopes checks whether other chemicals were in the blast
items.summary: Snopes published a Nov 25 piece asking whether the Army planned to detonate chemicals other than lead azide, tied to a redacted memo. The page could not be opened, so its findings are unknown here.
items.assessment: Redacted permit sections were already a petition demand. This shows the redaction question became its own claim.

items.headline: Army blows up degraded lead azide, air monitors find no lead
items.summary: The Army destroyed 68 drums of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in two blasts around 9am CT Wednesday. A joint FEMA and Army statement said air monitors showed no detectable lead, and the all clear came that evening. Surface sampling is underway with no results yet.
items.assessment: Zero airborne lead answers the plume question but not the ground question. Settled dust on soil, playgrounds and farms is what Iowa HHS and outside scientists say will decide health risk.
items.source: Washington Examiner via KhanList; AP via Christian Index

items.headline: Appeals court let the Army proceed, calling a random blast worse
items.summary: The 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals briefly paused the EPA permit on Nov 19, then lifted that pause on Nov 23. It acknowledged real risks in the planned blast but found an uncontrolled explosion more harmful.
items.assessment: The court ruled only on an emergency stay. The groups' underlying challenge to the permit may still be live, and its outcome could shape how EPA writes future emergency permits.

items.headline: Justice Department said the Army could blast without its permit
items.summary: In a Nov 22 court notice, the Justice Department said the Army would proceed even without the EPA permit. It cited an emergency exemption in EPA rules and said freezing weather sharply raised the risk of an accidental blast. The Army said it would still follow the permit's terms.
items.assessment: This filing signaled the court stay might not have stopped the blast. It raises a legal question about how much a court can check the military in a declared emergency.

items.headline: Lawsuit says EPA skipped safer options and set a weak cleanup bar
items.summary: The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, represented by Earthjustice, argued the EPA permit ignored mobile treatment units and a neutralization product EPA itself lists for lead azide. They said EPA skipped a 45 day comment period. They said its soil cleanup level of 800 parts per million is four times EPA's current 200 level.
items.assessment: The cleanup threshold matters more now than the blast. Whichever number EPA uses decides which yards and fields get cleaned.

items.headline: Iowa and Illinois officials say they learned late
items.summary: Gov. Kim Reynolds' office says the state learned of the blast plan on Nov 16, the day after the Army's public advisory. Illinois EPA said EPA Region 7 never notified it. The Army says it held an October open house and met Middletown officials Nov 12.
items.assessment: The drums were found in March and EPA posted storage permit notices in May and July. The gap was in telling states and residents about the blast plan itself, which came eight days before the first date.
items.source: Iowa Public Radio; Illinois Department of Public Health

items.headline: Iowa holds off on mass blood lead testing
items.summary: Iowa's health department said it does not recommend widespread blood lead tests just for living near the plant. It will issue targeted advice once soil and dust results come in. It said the airborne all clear does not end precautions about settled dust.
items.assessment: This makes the coming soil results the real trigger for health action. Families should keep wet cleaning play areas until those numbers are public.

items.headline: Trump paused the blast, then praised the result
items.summary: On Nov 23 President Trump said he ordered the military to wait for the appeals court and governor elect Rob Sand. The court cleared it that day. After the blast Trump posted that the Army's mitigation far exceeded expectations.
items.assessment: Giving an incoming Democratic governor a say was unusual. It also gave Sand shared ownership of the outcome before he takes office.

items.headline: Iowa members of Congress split on the timing
items.summary: Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks backed the Army plan because of the risk of an accidental explosion. Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democratic Rep. elect Christina Bohannan asked for a delay so residents could get clearer answers. Democrat Josh Turek asked for a pause until the risks were explained.
items.assessment: The split did not follow party lines. It ran between members who stressed the explosion risk and those who stressed public notice.

items.headline: Plant has a long pollution and compliance record
items.summary: The plant has been on the Superfund list since 1989 for explosives pollution. Nearby wells showed the explosive RDX in the 1990s. In 2024 the Army and operator American Ordnance paid $39,311 to EPA over 2023 hazardous waste violations, including open burning above permit limits.
items.assessment: This history helps explain local distrust of Army assurances. It also shows the plant already had treatment equipment that critics say deserved a closer look.
items.source: KILJ radio; EPA docket; Iowa DNR

items.headline: EPA reports zero airborne lead after Army blast, soil results pending
items.summary: The Army detonated about 5 tons of degraded lead azide at its Middletown, Iowa, plant on Nov 25. EPA says its real time air monitors detected no airborne lead more than five hours later. Soil and water results are still pending.
items.assessment: Zero in the air hours later does not settle the main question. Lead from a blast settles fast, so surface dust tests matter more than air readings.

items.headline: Iowa health agency holds off on blood lead testing until soil results
items.summary: Iowa's health department said on Nov 24 it is not urging blood lead tests just for living in the plume area. It will target testing once environmental sampling is in. It asked the CDC for field epidemiology help.
items.assessment: This makes the soil and surface data the trigger for everything else. Any delay in releasing it delays family health decisions.

items.headline: USDA projected about 350 farms under the expected lead plume
items.summary: Iowa's health department cited a USDA estimate that about 350 farms sat under the expected plume path. It stressed this is not confirmed contamination. Farmers were pointed to the state agriculture department and USDA for advice.
items.assessment: It is the clearest official count of farms at stake. No packer, dairy or egg buyer response has surfaced yet.

items.headline: Iowa State experts told farmers to pull cattle off pasture and ponds
items.summary: Iowa State University's beef and pork centers advised moving cattle off pasture and pond water and covering feed and water. They also said to take soil, forage or blood samples before and after the blast. Lead poisoning signs in cattle include blindness, tremors and sudden death.
items.assessment: Baseline samples taken before the blast are what will let a farmer prove harm later, including in an Army claim.

items.headline: Plant's 1970s open air detonation sent about a quarter of the lead azide airborne
items.summary: KWQC reports that the plant last destroyed lead azide this way in the 1970s, in the open air. About 25 percent of the material went into the air then. This time the Army used sand walls, water tanks, gel blocks and foam.
items.assessment: It is the only local precedent found. It shows why the containment layers mattered, and why sampling now must prove they worked.

items.headline: University of Iowa experts called the Army plume map a colored blob
items.summary: Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a University of Iowa environmental health professor, said the Army map showed no projected dust amounts on the ground. He urged testing playgrounds every few days for a month. His colleague Peter Thorne warned that hosing off dust just moves lead into soil and water.
items.assessment: The Army advice to rinse surfaces moves the lead rather than removing it. That shifts the question to soil and runoff testing.

items.headline: EPA had issued emergency storage permits for the lead azide since April
items.summary: EPA public notices show two emergency permits, from April 2 and July 1, letting the Army keep the unstable lead azide where its normal permit did not allow. The detonation permit came only on Nov 13. The governor's office says it learned of the plan Nov 16.
items.assessment: Federal regulators knew for about seven months. That gap is likely to drive any oversight or legal fight now.

items.headline: Purdue engineer Andrew Whelton weighs in on lead dose risk
items.summary: Andrew Whelton, a Purdue environmental engineering professor, told AP that high lead doses over a short time can cause poisoning. University of Iowa researchers said long term low doses mainly threaten brain development in young children.
items.assessment: Whelton led independent testing after the 2023 East Palestine train derailment. His team's data, if published, would be the first independent check here.

items.headline: The Intercept says the Army's hose it off advice falls short
items.summary: The Intercept, an investigative outlet, reported the Army told residents to hose off lead dust. University of Iowa scientists said that just moves lead into soil and water, and one called the situation neglect. The piece places it in a record of Army lead problems in housing, armories and ranges.
items.assessment: This was the earliest outlet to press the question of how long the Army sat on the problem. That question now drives both left and right criticism.
items.support: Two named University of Iowa experts say the modeling skipped settled dust and the cleanup advice lacks evidence.
items.against: The Army says it expects no long term health effects and the EPA permit requires sampling, cleanup and reporting.

items.headline: Common Dreams frames the blast as part of a cycle of military pollution
items.summary: Common Dreams, a progressive news site, gathered critics on blast day. CodePink called it reckless. Earthjustice says the Army knew of deterioration since 2009. Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club leaders said neglect and poor communication caused the outcry.
items.assessment: The piece turns a local hazard into a case against the defense budget, which signals where antiwar groups will take this next.
items.support: Earthjustice's 2009 timeline and the late notice to the governor support the neglect argument.
items.against: CodePink's Gaza munitions link is not verified in the piece. Officials say the blast went to plan with zero airborne lead.

items.headline: AlterNet stresses that Iowa's Republican governor learned of the plan days before
items.summary: AlterNet, a progressive aggregator, citing The Washington Sun, said the Pentagon knew by April. Reynolds' office said it learned from a public Army advisory and got formal notice Nov 16. Illinois EPA said federal regulators never told it. Illinois' health director said no level of lead in the body is safe.
items.assessment: The headline leads with the governor's party. The substance is a federal notification failure across two states.
items.support: The governor's office and Illinois EPA confirmed the late notice on the record.
items.against: The Army says it first raised the plan with Middletown residents at a mid October meeting.

items.headline: ZeroHedge casts the incoming Democratic governor as the holdout
items.summary: ZeroHedge, a finance and politics aggregator, relayed Trump's post making the blast depend on Rob Sand and the appeals court. It also carried critics' points that a neutralization contract was canceled and that a court filing implied more danger than disclosed. Its headline said Sand refused to sign off. The pages are undated and their content places them around Nov 23 to 24.
items.assessment: ZeroHedge carried both the White House blame frame and the strongest neglect evidence, which most outlets on either side split apart.
items.support: Trump's own post set Sand's agreement as a condition, and a White House official criticized Sand publicly.
items.against: Sand said he declined to sign off or object and that the administration should decide based on its own experts' information.

items.headline: Ron Paul Institute essay predicts official spin, citing East Palestine
items.summary: Kurt Nimmo, a former Infowars editor, wrote that agencies will downplay harm, based on the 2023 Ohio derailment. The Ron Paul Institute, a libertarian antiwar group, reprinted it on blast day. He cites studies of East Palestine symptoms and a reported CDC message to clinicians.
items.assessment: It is the clearest statement of the distrust frame. Its evidence is about Ohio, not Iowa.
items.source: Ron Paul Institute (reprint of Another Day in the Empire)
items.support: Published studies and lawsuits document lasting complaints and response gaps after East Palestine.
items.against: Iowa air readings showed zero lead and the EPA permit requires published sampling. Several of the essay's Ohio claims are presented as alleged.

items.headline: Alex Jones Live reports a clean blast while its readers doubt it
items.summary: Alex Jones Live, a site tied to the Infowars host, relayed EPA's zero lead readings and drone clips from X. It quoted a public health commentator saying soil and water tests matter more than air. Commenters questioned whether monitors worked and accused the government of targeting the public.
items.assessment: The gap between the post's cautious tone and its comment section shows distrust running ahead of the outlet itself.
items.support: The Army's own plan calls for soil, water and sediment testing, which supports the point that air data is incomplete.
items.against: EPA said all monitors read zero, and other commenters noted lead falls quickly rather than staying airborne.

items.headline: Epoch Times leans on officials to report no lead in the air
items.summary: The Epoch Times, a conservative paper, reported zero airborne lead and said the visible plume was mostly foam. It said over 1,200 samples were taken before the blast. The piece quoted officials only, including the general who led the operation.
items.assessment: A right leaning outlet ran the most reassuring account, which cuts against a simple left versus right split on this story.
items.source: The Epoch Times (via The Thinking Conservative)
items.support: EPA, Army and ATF officials all reported a complete and contained detonation.
items.against: No independent experts were quoted, and soil and water results were not yet in.

baseRatesTitle: Past Cases and What Testing Later Showed

baseRates.cause: Fire melted and burned a lead roof and spire holding about 460 tonnes of lead
baseRates.howCauseWasFound: Health officials tested 1,222 children and found no fire related rise in blood lead. Every child with lead poisoning had another lead source. A soil study found downwind soil averaged about 430 mg/kg versus 240 elsewhere.
baseRates.source: Santé publique France; van Geen et al. 2020

baseRates.event: East Palestine, Ohio train derailment vent and burn
baseRates.cause: Deliberate release and burn of vinyl chloride after a derailment
baseRates.howCauseWasFound: EPA soil tests at 146 spots found most dioxin and related results within normal background ranges. Surface and deeper soil looked alike, suggesting the compounds predated the burn.
baseRates.source: EPA East Palestine soil sampling page

baseRates.event: Camp Minden, Louisiana M6 propellant disposal
baseRates.cause: About 7,500 tons of degrading artillery propellant. A planned open air burn met public opposition.
baseRates.howCauseWasFound: After protests the propellant was burned in a closed chamber with pollution controls. The closure plan says no releases were recorded. An Aug 2016 EPA air check found all pollutants below federal standards.
baseRates.source: Louisiana National Guard closure plan; EPA air summary; NPR

baseRates.event: Radford Army Ammunition Plant open burning, Virginia
baseRates.cause: Routine open burning of explosive waste
baseRates.howCauseWasFound: Drone sampling found most pollutants below model estimates. Lead was about five times higher than expected in one burn type, arsenic 37.5 times.

baseRates.cause: Decades of emissions and ore spills from the Doe Run lead smelter
baseRates.howCauseWasFound: Yard soil reached 33,100 ppm lead. 28 percent of tested young children had elevated blood lead in 2001 and 14 percent in 2002. Yards above 400 ppm were dug out and nearby homes were bought out.

baseRates.event: Iowa Army Ammunition Plant open air lead azide detonation
baseRates.cause: Disposal of lead azide by open air detonation with no containment
baseRates.howCauseWasFound: KWQC reports about 25 percent of the material went into the air. No later soil test results were found in this run.

baseRates.event: Iowa Army Ammunition Plant explosives contamination of groundwater
baseRates.cause: Decades of munitions loading and waste disposal on site
baseRates.howCauseWasFound: State sampling found TNT in five off site wells and RDX above health advisory in five wells in 1992 to 1993. Groundwater RDX trends fell in 2007 to 2010 tests. The Army supplies bottled water to affected homes.

baseRates.event: Lead paint in Army family housing
baseRates.cause: Deteriorating lead paint in military housing
baseRates.howCauseWasFound: A 2018 Reuters investigation documented more than 1,000 elevated child blood lead tests at one Army medical center.

baseRates.event: Lead at National Guard indoor firing ranges
baseRates.cause: Lead from firing ranges not properly remediated
baseRates.howCauseWasFound: An Army audit found 73 of 83 indoor ranges in three states lacked thorough cleanup or lead hazard checks. Some used pressure washing the audit warned against.

baseRates.cause: Leftover lead from old firing ranges in armories
baseRates.howCauseWasFound: A 2024 Intercept investigation found the Army National Guard did not adequately clean up lead in armories.

baseRates.event: Kansas City World Cup FanFest fireworks (EPA comparison)
baseRates.howCauseWasFound: EPA Administrator Zeldin claims the fireworks produced about 10 times more particulate matter than the Iowa blast. This is an agency claim not independently checked.

baseRatesNote: Comparable disposals, fires and contamination cases, and what follow up testing found. Most big events produced reassuring air data first and harder soil questions later. Herculaneum is the case where soil and blood tests found serious harm.

international.what: CCTV, the state broadcaster, ran a piece republished on Sina stressing toxic chemicals, a cloud that could travel about 160 km, and risk to pregnant women and children. A Weibo creator post with drone video carried the same 160 km headline.
international.source: CCTV and a Weibo creator, both via Sina

international.what: China Times reported official safety claims next to residents' unease and critics asking why the drums sat since 2009. Public broadcaster PTS reported Vance blaming the Obama administration and said the Army ordered a nationwide storage safety review.
The Epoch Times Chinese edition led with Trump's praise and joking onlookers. Kanzhongguo (Vision Times) ran a straight wire compilation stressing that air results were preliminary.
international.source: Epoch Times Chinese edition and Kanzhongguo

international.what: Moskovsky Komsomolets rewrites on Mail.ru and Rambler said the Army timed the blast to Thanksgiving and that a cloud could spread 160 km. The body text said tens of kilometers. Kommersant earlier framed it as the Army pushing ahead despite a court. RBC said the Army destroyed its whole stock.
international.source: MK via Mail.ru and Rambler, Kommersant, RBC

international.what: TRT's Russian language service, run by Turkey's state broadcaster, stressed protests, 17 years of storage and that air sensors do not rule out soil contamination.

Demócrata ran a wire story relaying Army, FEMA and ATF statements. It quoted HHS official Sean Kaufman saying misinformation is as dangerous as lead.
CBC headlined that the Army called the blast a success despite toxic plume concerns. Seen in search only, page did not load.
IBTimes UK ran a piece on Iowa families fearing for safety ahead of Thanksgiving. Seen in search only.

international.country: Puerto Rico (US territory, Spanish language press)

JournalArta, an Indonesia based site with an English global edition, led with dust that could travel 100 miles, evacuations and school closures. It included the Army's reasoning lower down.

stateNarratives.claim: CCTV claims the US Army set off toxic chemicals whose smoke could spread about 160 km, endangering pregnant women and children.
stateNarratives.counterpoint: The 160 km figure was the Army's worst case notice zone. EPA found no airborne lead after the blast.

stateNarratives.claim: TRT says the stockpile sat 17 years and degraded, and that clean air readings do not rule out soil or water contamination.
stateNarratives.counterpoint: EPA has more than 1,000 ground samples in labs and says it will publish results. None show contamination so far.

stateNarratives.claim: PTS says the Army ordered a nationwide safety review of weapons storage after the blast.
stateNarratives.relatedTo: Iowa lead azide detonation, other degraded munitions stockpiles
